title: Regular Expressions
summary: A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern that describes a set of strings. JavaScript has a built-in `RegExp` type for matching, searching, and replacing text using compact pattern syntax for character classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups.

subtopics.title: Regex literals vs the RegExp constructor
subtopics.explanation: You can write a pattern as a literal between slashes, /pattern/flags, which is compiled once when the script loads — best when the pattern is fixed. The RegExp constructor, new RegExp('pattern', 'flags'), builds a regex from a string at runtime, which you need when the pattern is dynamic (built from a variable). With the constructor, remember each backslash must itself be escaped in the string.
subtopics.example:
const a = /\d+/g;
const b = new RegExp('\\d+', 'g'); // same pattern, built from a string

subtopics.title: Character classes
subtopics.explanation: A character class matches one character from a set. Square brackets define your own set, like [aeiou] for a vowel or [a-z] for a lowercase letter, and a leading caret negates it: [^0-9] is any non-digit. Shorthand classes cover common sets: \d (digit), \w (word character: letters, digits, underscore), \s (whitespace), and their uppercase negations \D, \W, \S. A bare dot . matches any character except a newline.
subtopics.example:
/[A-Za-z]/   // one letter
/\d/         // one digit
/[^\s]/      // one non-whitespace character

subtopics.title: Quantifiers
subtopics.explanation: Quantifiers say how many times the preceding item may repeat. * means zero or more, + means one or more, and ? means zero or one (optional). Curly braces give exact counts: {3} is exactly three, {2,4} is two to four, {2,} is two or more. By default quantifiers are greedy (match as much as possible); add a ? to make them lazy (match as little as possible), as in .*?.
subtopics.example:
/\d{3}/      // exactly three digits
/colou?r/    // 'color' or 'colour'
/<.+?>/      // lazy: shortest tag match

subtopics.title: Anchors
subtopics.explanation: Anchors match positions, not characters. ^ asserts the start of the string (or line in multiline mode), $ asserts the end. Using both, like /^\d+$/, forces the entire string to match the pattern rather than just containing it. The word boundary \b matches the edge between a word character and a non-word character, useful for whole-word matches.
subtopics.example:
/^abc$/      // the string is exactly 'abc'
/\bcat\b/    // the whole word 'cat', not 'category'

subtopics.title: Groups and capturing
subtopics.explanation: Parentheses group part of a pattern so quantifiers and alternation (|) apply to the whole group, and they capture the matched text for later use. Captured groups are numbered and returned by match/exec; named groups (?<name>...) make them readable. A non-capturing group (?:...) groups without saving the match, which is slightly cheaper when you only need grouping.
subtopics.example:
/(\d{4})-(\d{2})/        // two numbered capture groups
/(?<year>\d{4})/          // a named group
/(?:ab)+/                 // group without capturing

subtopics.title: Flags
subtopics.explanation: Flags change how the whole regex behaves. g (global) finds all matches instead of just the first and is required for replaceAll-style and matchAll behavior. i (ignore case) makes matching case-insensitive. m (multiline) makes ^ and $ match at line boundaries within the string. Other flags include s (dotAll, so . also matches newlines) and u (unicode).
subtopics.example:
/error/gi    // every 'error', any case
/^\d+$/m     // each line is all digits

subtopics.title: test, match, replace, matchAll
subtopics.explanation: RegExp.prototype.test(str) returns a boolean — ideal for validation. String.prototype.match returns the first match (or all matches with the g flag), while matchAll returns an iterator of every match WITH capture groups. replace swaps matched text, supporting $1 backreferences or a replacer function; with a global regex it replaces every occurrence. Beware: a regex with the g flag is stateful (lastIndex) when reused with test/exec.
subtopics.example:
/\d+/.test('a1');                 // true
'a1 b2'.match(/\d+/g);            // ['1','2']
'a1 b2'.replace(/\d/g, '#');      // 'a# b#'
[...'a1 b2'.matchAll(/(\d)/g)];   // matches with groups

subtopics.title: Lookahead (a note)
subtopics.explanation: A lookahead asserts what follows without consuming it. Positive lookahead (?=...) matches a position only if the pattern ahead matches; negative lookahead (?!...) matches only if it does NOT. A common use is password rules: assert at least one digit somewhere ahead without removing it from the match. (JavaScript also supports lookbehind (?<=...) / (?<!...) in modern engines.)
subtopics.example:
/\d(?=px)/    // a digit followed by 'px', but 'px' is not captured
/^(?=.*\d).{8,}$/ // 8+ chars containing at least one digit

subtopics.title: Escaping special characters
subtopics.explanation: Characters like . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ | \ have special meaning in regex. To match them literally, prefix with a backslash: \. matches a real dot, \$ a real dollar sign. Inside the RegExp constructor's string form you must double the backslash (\\.). When building a regex from arbitrary user input, escape it first to avoid both bugs and ReDoS risks.
subtopics.example:
/\./         // a literal dot
/\$\d+/      // a dollar sign followed by digits

foundations.overview: Regular expressions let you describe text patterns declaratively and then test, search, extract, or replace matching text. JavaScript exposes them through the RegExp object and several String/RegExp methods. The skill is reading and composing the small set of building blocks — classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups, and flags — into precise patterns.
foundations.formalDefinition: A regular expression is a sequence of characters that defines a search pattern over strings, evaluated by a regex engine that attempts to match the pattern against input using backtracking. In JavaScript a regex is a RegExp object, created via a /.../ literal or new RegExp().
foundations.whyItMatters: Regex is the most compact tool for validation (emails, phone numbers), parsing and extraction (pulling fields from text/logs), search-and-replace (formatting, sanitizing), and routing. It appears constantly in real code and in interviews because it tests precise, rule-based thinking.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a regex as a tiny program that walks the input one position at a time, trying to satisfy each part of the pattern in order, and backtracking when a path fails. Anchors check positions, character classes consume one character, and quantifiers control repetition.
foundations.browserPerspective: JavaScript engines compile a regex to an internal automaton/backtracking matcher. A literal regex is compiled once; the g/y flags make a regex stateful via lastIndex, which the engine updates between exec/test calls so iteration can resume.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Form validation, search highlighting, slugifying titles, parsing query strings, extracting tokens from logs, sanitizing input, and find-and-replace in editors all lean on regex.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct validation regex improves data quality and reduces support load, while a buggy or catastrophically slow pattern (ReDoS) can corrupt data or hang a request thread, hurting reliability.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing regex turns multi-line parsing loops into a single expressive line, but over-relying on it for structured formats (HTML, deeply nested data) creates fragile code — knowing the limits is part of the skill.
foundations.performanceImpact: Most patterns are fast, but nested quantifiers on ambiguous input can cause catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), turning a match into exponential time. Anchoring, avoiding overlapping quantifiers, and limiting input size mitigate this.
commonUseCases: Validating input formats like emails, phone numbers, and postal codes
Extracting fields or tokens from text and logs with capture groups
Splitting or scanning strings by complex delimiters

commonMisconceptions.myth: A single regex can fully validate every real email address.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The full email spec is far too complex for a practical regex; teams use a pragmatic pattern plus a verification email instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: test() on a global regex is stateless and safe to reuse.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A regex with the g (or y) flag tracks lastIndex, so repeated test/exec calls on the same regex advance through the string and can give surprising results.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Regex is the right tool for parsing HTML/JSON.
commonMisconceptions.reality: These are nested, recursive formats; regex is not a parser and breaks on edge cases — use a real parser/DOM instead.

visualExplorer.title: How the engine matches a pattern
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how /^\d{3}-\d{4}$/ matches the string '123-4567'.

config.intro: Watch the engine walk '123-4567' against the pattern, position by position.

steps.name: Anchor at start (^)
steps.detail: Assert we are at the start of the string before consuming anything.

steps.name: Match the literal -
steps.detail: The next character must be a hyphen; '-' matches.

steps.name: Anchor at end ($)
steps.detail: Assert we are at the end of the string — no leftover characters, so the whole string matches.

interactiveExamples.title: Validate with test()
interactiveExamples.explanation: test() returns true/false, perfect for checking whether a string fits a pattern. Anchors ^ and $ ensure the whole string matches, not just a part.

sandbox.code:
const zip = /^\d{5}$/; // exactly five digits, start to end

console.log(zip.test('90210')); // true
console.log(zip.test('9021'));  // false (too short)
console.log(zip.test('90210x'));// false (extra char)
console.log(zip.test('a90210'));// false (anchored)

interactiveExamples.title: Extract groups with matchAll
interactiveExamples.explanation: Capture groups pull out parts of each match. With the g flag, matchAll yields every match plus its captured groups.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Logs each match with its year/month, then 'Order 01/2024 and order 12/2025'.

codeLab.title: Slugify a title
codeLab.instructions: Implement slugify(title) that lowercases the string, replaces any run of non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen, and trims leading/trailing hyphens. Use regex with the g flag.
hints: [^a-z0-9]+ matches one or more non-alphanumeric characters; the + collapses runs.
Trim with /^-+|-+$/g after replacing, to remove hyphens at the edges.

debuggingLab.title: Stateful global regex with test()
debuggingLab.symptom: Calling test() repeatedly on the same string alternates between true and false instead of always returning true.

brokenCode.code:
const re = /\d+/g; // note the g flag

console.log(re.test('abc123')); // true
console.log(re.test('abc123')); // false (!)
console.log(re.test('abc123')); // true again
// the result flips on every call

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A regex with the g (or y) flag is stateful: each successful test/exec updates re.lastIndex to where the previous match ended. The second test() resumes from after '123', finds nothing, returns false, and resets lastIndex to 0 — so the third call matches again. The flag, not the input, is the culprit.
commonMistakes: Reusing a single global regex across test() calls and expecting statelessness.
Forgetting that lastIndex persists between calls on the same RegExp object.
Using the g flag with test() when you only need a boolean.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make every call return true for the same matching string.

solution.code:
const re = /\d+/; // drop the g flag for boolean checks

console.log(re.test('abc123')); // true
console.log(re.test('abc123')); // true
console.log(re.test('abc123')); // true
// Alternatively keep g but reset: re.lastIndex = 0 before each test

theory.question: What is the difference between a regex literal and the RegExp constructor?
theory.directAnswer: A literal /pattern/flags is written directly in source and compiled once when the code is parsed — use it for fixed patterns. new RegExp('pattern', 'flags') builds a regex from a string at runtime — use it when the pattern is dynamic. In the constructor, every backslash must be escaped again because it lives inside a JavaScript string, so \d becomes '\\d'.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to create a RegExp object: inline literal syntax versus a constructor that takes string arguments.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Literals are concise and compiled once; the constructor exists so patterns can be assembled from variables at runtime.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The literal is compiled when the script loads; the constructor compiles its string argument each time it runs, interpreting the string's escape sequences first, which is why backslashes must be doubled.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right form avoids subtle escaping bugs and unnecessary recompilation, and the double-backslash gotcha is a frequent interview trap.
theory.realWorldExample: Building a search regex from a user's query at runtime requires new RegExp(escape(query), 'gi'); a fixed email check uses a literal.

nestedTopics.title: Compile time
nestedTopics.explanation: Literals compile once; the constructor compiles per call.

nestedTopics.title: Double escaping
nestedTopics.explanation: Constructor strings need \\ for one regex backslash.

nestedTopics.title: Dynamic patterns
nestedTopics.explanation: Only the constructor can build a pattern from a variable.

followUps.question: How do you safely build a regex from user input?
followUps.answer: Escape the input first (replace regex metacharacters with their backslashed forms) before passing it to new RegExp, to prevent broken patterns and ReDoS.

theory.question: What do the g, i, and m flags do, and how do they change matching?
theory.directAnswer: g (global) finds all matches rather than stopping at the first and enables matchAll and replace-all behavior, but makes the regex stateful via lastIndex. i (ignore case) makes letters match regardless of case. m (multiline) makes the anchors ^ and $ match at the start/end of each line within the string instead of only the whole string.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Flags appended after the closing slash that modify the regex's matching behavior globally.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: They let one pattern serve different needs — all matches vs first, case sensitivity, and line-oriented anchoring — without changing the pattern itself.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: g and y track lastIndex to resume scanning; i folds case during comparison; m redefines ^ and $ to match at newline boundaries; s (dotAll) lets . match newlines.

theory.whyImportant: Flag misuse causes real bugs (stateful test(), anchors not matching per line), making this a practical, frequently asked topic.
theory.realWorldExample: Highlighting every search term uses g+i; validating that each line of input is all digits uses m with /^\d+$/m.

nestedTopics.title: Multiline anchors
nestedTopics.explanation: m makes ^ and $ match per line.

followUps.question: What does the s (dotAll) flag add?
followUps.answer: It makes the dot . also match newline characters, so a pattern can span multiple lines without explicitly matching \n.

scenario.question: A validation regex passes in tests but occasionally hangs the server on certain inputs. What is happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: That is catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): a pattern with nested or overlapping quantifiers, like (a+)+ or (.*)*, can explore exponentially many ways to match a non-matching input, so a crafted string makes the engine loop nearly forever. I'd rewrite the pattern to remove ambiguity (avoid nested quantifiers, anchor it, use possessive/atomic-style restructuring), bound the input length, and validate with safer constructs or a real parser.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A performance failure where backtracking turns matching into exponential-time work on adversarial input.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Backtracking engines try every combination when a quantified group can match the same text in multiple ways and the overall match ultimately fails.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Removing the ambiguity (so each character has only one way to be consumed) and anchoring the pattern collapses the search space back to linear time.

scenario.whyImportant: ReDoS is a genuine availability/security risk in input-handling code and a strong signal of regex depth.

nestedTopics.title: Catastrophic backtracking
nestedTopics.explanation: Ambiguous quantifiers cause exponential matching attempts.

nestedTopics.title: Mitigations
nestedTopics.explanation: Anchor, de-ambiguate, bound input length, prefer parsers for structured data.

followUps.question: How would you detect ReDoS-prone patterns before shipping?
followUps.answer: Use static analyzers/linters for dangerous regex shapes, run patterns against pathological inputs in tests, and enforce input length limits at the boundary.

coding.question: Write a function that extracts all hashtags from a string and returns them without the leading # symbol.
coding.thoughtProcess: A hashtag is a # followed by one or more word characters. I'll use a global regex with a capture group for the word part and matchAll to iterate every occurrence, collecting group 1 from each match. A word boundary keeps it tidy and \w covers letters, digits, and underscore.
coding.lineByLine: /#(\w+)/g matches a # then captures one or more word characters; the g flag makes matchAll return every hashtag. Spreading the iterator gives an array of match objects, and m[1] is the captured text without the #. The result is a clean array of tag names.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the input string.

alternativeApproaches.title: match without groups, then strip
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use text.match(/#\w+/g) to get the full tags and slice off the # afterward.

followUps.question: How would you allow Unicode letters in hashtags?
followUps.answer: Use the u flag with a Unicode property escape like /#([\p{L}\p{N}_]+)/gu so non-ASCII letters and digits are included.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Regex sits at input boundaries — validation layers, parsers, sanitizers, and routers. A common pattern is to centralize reusable patterns (email, phone, slug) in one module so they are tested once and shared, rather than re-authored inline across the codebase.
productionDeepDive.performance: Compiling literals once and reusing them avoids per-call recompilation; the real risk is catastrophic backtracking on ambiguous patterns. Anchoring, avoiding nested quantifiers, bounding input length, and preferring linear-time constructs keep matching fast.
productionDeepDive.security: Regex is both a defense (input validation) and a liability (ReDoS denial-of-service). User-supplied patterns must be escaped before use, and patterns applied to user input must be reviewed for backtracking blowups; never use regex to 'sanitize' HTML — use a real sanitizer.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Hot-path validation (per request, per keystroke) benefits from pre-compiled, anchored patterns and short-circuit checks (length/format pre-filters) before heavier regex. Move expensive parsing off the request thread when input is large.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Complex regex is write-once, read-never without help: name patterns, add comments explaining intent, and split monster expressions into smaller, tested pieces. For structured formats, a parser is far more maintainable than a giant regex.
productionDeepDive.observability: Track validation failure rates and slow-match timings; a spike in regex execution time or a thread stall often signals a ReDoS attempt. Log which pattern and input length triggered slow matches.

caseStudies.problem: A naive validation regex with nested quantifiers hung request threads on crafted inputs (ReDoS).
caseStudies.solution: Rewrote patterns to remove ambiguity, anchored them, and added input length limits plus regex linting in CI.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly less 'clever' patterns vs. predictable linear-time matching.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat regex on untrusted input as a performance and security boundary, not just a convenience.

projectBuilder.summary: Build a small validation and text-utility module for a Todo app: validate email/phone fields, slugify todo titles, and highlight search matches — all powered by reusable, tested regex.
requirements: An email validator using a pragmatic anchored pattern
A phone validator that accepts common formats
A slugify and a search-highlight utility
projectBuilder.architecture: A validators module exporting named, pre-compiled regex and small functions; a textUtils module for slugify and highlight. The Todo UI imports them for form validation and search.

steps.title: Write the email validator
steps.instructions: Use an anchored pattern like /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/ and wrap it in isEmail(str).
steps.checkpoint: Valid addresses pass; missing @ or domain fails.

steps.title: Write the phone validator
steps.instructions: Accept digits with optional spaces/dashes, e.g. /^\+?\d[\d\s-]{7,}$/, in isPhone(str).

steps.title: Write slugify and highlight
steps.instructions: Slugify with /[^a-z0-9]+/g; highlight by wrapping matches via replace with the g and i flags.
steps.checkpoint: Titles become clean slugs; search terms get wrapped.

enhancements: Add Unicode-aware patterns with the u flag
Escape user search input before building the highlight regex
Add a ReDoS test with pathological inputs
interviewQuestions: Why is a fully spec-compliant email regex impractical, and what do teams do instead?
How do you safely build a search-highlight regex from user input?

keyTakeaways: A regex is a pattern over strings; create one with a /.../ literal (fixed, compiled once) or new RegExp(string) (dynamic, with doubled backslashes).
The core building blocks are character classes (\d, \w, [...]), quantifiers (*, +, ?, {n,m}), anchors (^, $, \b), and groups ((...), (?:...), (?<name>...)).
Flags reshape matching: g for all matches (and stateful lastIndex), i for case-insensitivity, m for per-line anchors, s for dotAll.
Use test() for validation, match/matchAll for extraction (matchAll keeps groups), and replace for substitution with $1 or a function.
Escape metacharacters and user input, beware catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), and reach for a real parser instead of regex for nested formats like HTML.
